cards.title: Structure a GA4 account for an ecommerce store
cards.summary: Decide account, property and data stream structure based on whether your storefront, checkout and subdomains form one user journey.
cards.use_when: Setting up GA4 for a store that spans several domains (e.g. main shop domain plus a separate checkout or landing domains) and you need to decide how many properties and streams to create.
steps: Treat the GA4 account as the organization: for a single business, one account is usually enough.

Create one property per distinct user journey you want measured together. If a shopper moves from your main site to a dedicated checkout domain and then purchases, use ONE property for both so the journey is visible in one place.
If your sites are separate business lines whose data you never want combined (e.g. two unrelated product ranges), give each its own property so data is not mixed.
Inside a property, use one web data stream even for multiple websites — Google recommends one web stream across sites rather than a stream per domain.
Which domain you type when creating the web stream is not critical; the stream still works for the other domains in the property.
When multiple domains are in one property, configure cross-domain tracking in the data stream settings so sessions are not split when visitors jump domains.
Select reporting time zone and currency at property creation — these match where the business is, not the individual shopper.
Choose business objectives at setup; they only change which report collections are unlocked. The presenter prefers the older report layout, so pick objectives you'll actually use or select 'other'.
Verify the current interface wording in the GA4 admin panel before following these steps, as Google changes report collection names.
caveats: Report collection names differ depending on the business objectives selected and change over time; content is similar but labels vary.
GA4 takes roughly 24–48 hours to fully process data, so a fresh property or new custom dimensions will not appear in standard reports immediately.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Install the GA4 tag: CMS, hardcode, or GTM
cards.summary: Choose between a CMS tracking-ID field, developer-installed code, or Google Tag Manager for deploying GA4 on an ecommerce site.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to deploy GA4 (and later ecommerce event tags) on your storefront, especially when you lack developer time or need to add vendor tags.
steps: Option 1 — built-in integration: many ecommerce platforms have a field for the measurement ID (starts with 'G-'). Find it in GA4 under Admin > Data Streams > your web stream > Measurement ID, paste it into the platform field, and the platform installs GA4 for you.
Option 2 — custom site: hand the Google tag snippet to a developer to add to every page. Google recommends the <head> section; the <body> also works if the head is not feasible.

Option 3 — Google Tag Manager: create a container at tagmanager.google.com, install the first GTM container code on all pages (the second snippet can be ignored), then add a Google tag with your measurement ID inside GTM.
A container needs its code on every page for the Google tag to activate everywhere, so this is the critical developer handoff.
GTM's main advantage is managing many tags (GA4, Meta pixel, LinkedIn insight tag) without repeated developer involvement — useful when you need to iterate on ecommerce event tracking.
After publishing in GTM, GA4 starts collecting data; allow 24–48 hours before trusting new reports.
caveats: GTM has a learning curve; the presenter's stated preference for GTM is his opinion, not a universal requirement.
Exact GTM and GA4 button labels change; verify the current interface before instructing a developer.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Test a GA4 tag with GTM Preview and DebugView
cards.summary: Run the GTM preview → DebugView sequence to confirm a tag fires and GA4 receives the event and its parameters before publishing.
cards.use_when: Validating any new GA4 tracking tag (ecommerce events, custom events) on your store before publishing it to live shoppers.
steps: In GTM click Preview, enter the store URL, and click Connect; the site opens in a new tab with tag assistant connected.
Trigger the action you want to measure if needed (for a page-load tag, just visiting is enough) and inspect the event in the preview panel — confirm your tag fired.
Open GA4 in another tab: Admin > Debug View. Confirm the events arrive (e.g. page_view, scroll, session_start) and that parameters such as page location and URL match.
For custom events, click into the event in DebugView and verify the custom parameters you attached (e.g. menu item name/URL) are present, not just the default ones.
Only after both GTM preview and DebugView confirm receipt, go back to GTM and Submit / Publish the container version.
Re-enable Preview each time you restart a GTM session if the preview disconnects.
caveats: A preview-mode 'unknown tag type' warning can be a preview bug — tags can still work correctly.
Newly published events and custom dimensions can take 24–48 hours to surface in standard GA4 reports, so DebugView is the fast check, not the report.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Read acquisition reports: first touch vs session
cards.summary: Distinguish user acquisition (first source ever) from traffic acquisition (per session) to answer the right question about store traffic.
cards.use_when: Deciding which channel or campaign drove purchases and revenue for your store, and avoiding misreading first-touch attribution as current-session attribution.
steps: Use User Acquisition to see the FIRST source that ever acquired a visitor — a user acquired months ago by organic search stays in the organic row for all later sessions.
Use Traffic Acquisition for per-session data, which most marketers actually want: group traffic sources, then drill into Session source/medium.
Add sessions, then revenue, as metrics and sort by the metric you care about — e.g. sort by revenue to see which sources actually paid off, not just which drove volume.
Add Session campaign name via the plus button (dimension) to break revenue down by individual campaign, e.g. to find which email newsletter generated the most revenue.

Use quick filters to isolate a channel: filter Session medium exactly matches email, or combine Session medium = cpc with Session source contains facebook.com to see paid social campaigns and their revenue.
Change chart granularity (day vs week) and the date range to read trends; clearing rows can blank a chart, so reselect rows or click plot rows to restore data.
caveats: Assertion that 'most marketers want traffic acquisition' is the presenter's opinion.
The default chart shows only the top five sources; deselect or plot specific rows to see others.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Use the ecommerce purchases report for product decisions
cards.summary: Read item views, add-to-carts, purchases and item revenue per product to find merchandising winners and drop-off points.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and product-selection decisions — spotting products with strong views but weak add-to-cart or purchase rates, or identifying top revenue items.
steps: Open the Monetization report (might be labeled revenue in your layout) and go to E-commerce purchases.
Read the columns per item: how often the product was viewed, added to cart, purchased, and item revenue. Sorting by item revenue surfaces top performers (e.g. a best-selling sweater).
Use gaps between view → add-to-cart → purchase as a signal: a product viewed a lot but rarely bought may have pricing, imagery, or PDP-copy issues worth testing.
Treat this data as available ONLY if you or your platform sends view_item / add_to_cart / purchase events with product and revenue parameters — GA4 does not track this out of the box.
If the data is missing, either ask your platform about its GA4 ecommerce integration or have a developer/GTM send the events, then allow 24–48 hours for processing.
caveats: Out-of-the-box GA4 does not send ecommerce events; without configuration this report is empty or partial.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Diagnose checkout drop-off by device or browser
cards.summary: Use the checkout journey report with breakdown dimensions to find where and on which devices/browsers shoppers abandon checkout.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the cart and checkout flow — locating funnel steps that lose the most shoppers and checking whether a specific browser/device has a technical problem.
steps: Open the checkout journey report to see drop-off between steps: users who started checkout, added shipping info, added payment info, then purchased.
Change the breakdown dimension to Device category to compare completion rates across desktop, mobile and tablet.
Switch the breakdown to Browser and scan for a step where one browser drops off significantly more — that pattern suggests a technical bug rather than a UX preference.
Investigate the suspect step in that browser (e.g. reproduce the failing checkout) before assuming it is a design issue.
Repeat across steps to prioritise which fix affects the most lost orders.
caveats: Requires ecommerce events (begin_checkout, add_shipping_info, add_payment_info, purchase) to be configured; GA4 does not collect these automatically.
A higher drop-off for one browser is a hypothesis pointing to a bug, not proof.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Landing page vs pages and screens report
cards.summary: Use the landing-page report for session entry pages and pages-and-screens for total page views, and understand why revenue in the pages report can mislead.
cards.use_when: Evaluating which entry pages (homepage, collections, checkout URL) start sessions and drive revenue, versus measuring overall page popularity.
steps: Use the Landing page report to see the FIRST page of each session and revenue attributed to those entry sessions — useful for judging which entry points (homepage, new arrivals, clearance) actually produce revenue.
Use Pages and screens for total page views regardless of position in the session, plus users and active users per page.

Sort Pages and screens by views or users to find the most-visited pages; be aware revenue in this report is attributed to the page where the conversion occurred, so almost all revenue lands on checkout — the presenter considers revenue unhelpful here.
Interpret 'active users': a user who spent at least 10 seconds, converted (a key event), viewed 2+ pages in a session, or is a new user.

Expect checkout URLs to appear as landing pages when a session expires mid-purchase — a visitor who leaves after adding to cart and returns later can start a new session with checkout as the landing page.
To reduce that false signal, consider raising the default session timeout (see the session-timeout card).
caveats: Revenue in the pages-and-screens report is attributed to the conversion page, making it near-useless for judging page value.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Mark key events and pick the right conversion metric
cards.summary: Distinguish plain events from key events (purchase, signup) and use them in acquisition and exploration reports to count real business outcomes.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ecommerce actions (purchase, newsletter signup, account creation) should count as conversions and where to read them by traffic source.
steps: Treat every interaction GA4 records as an event; mark business-critical ones (purchase, signup) as key events.
In acquisition reports, use the event-count selector to count a specific event (e.g. purchase) by traffic source, and use the key-events section for events you have promoted.
Remember User Acquisition counts key events on a first-touch basis, so a repeat buyer counts under the original acquisition source.
When building explorations, filter by event name (exactly matches purchase) to isolate the action and avoid mixing in irrelevant events.
Only mark as key the actions that map to revenue or clear value — over-marking dilutes the signal.
caveats: Key events are only available once the underlying event is actually being sent; GA4 does not detect purchases without configuration.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Build a free-form exploration for product/device decisions
cards.summary: Create free-form explorations with dimensions as rows/columns and metrics as values to cross-tab store performance, e.g. revenue by country and device.
cards.use_when: Answering a specific merchandising or targeting question — e.g. which countries or device categories generate the most purchase revenue — beyond what standard reports allow.
steps: Open Explore, choose Free form (blank), and note the three-pane layout: Variables (dimensions, metrics, segments), Settings, and the output table.
Add dimensions you will use (e.g. Device category, Country) and metrics (e.g. purchase revenue) via the plus buttons, then confirm.
Drag dimensions into Rows and Columns, and the metric into Values; double-clicking a dimension also adds it.
Read the resulting table, e.g. revenue by country split into desktop/mobile/tablet, then switch visualization between bar chart, heat map (darker = higher), and plain table.
Share a finished exploration via the share icon so other property users can see it.
caveats: Explorations are private to their creator by default; sharing is view-only — others must copy and modify their own version to change it.
Exploration data is limited by the property's data retention window (default 2 months).
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Mine site-search terms to find assortment gaps
cards.summary: Build a free-form exploration of site search terms and event counts to see what shoppers ask for and whether your catalogue answers it.
cards.use_when: Product selection and assortment planning — spotting search terms with high demand but no matching products, or reframing how products are named/merchandised.
steps: Open Explore, add a new free-form tab.
Add dimensions Event name and Search term, and metric Event count.
Put Search term in Rows and Event count in Values.

Filter Event name exactly matches the search-results event (the presenter's demo uses 'view search results') so the report stops mixing search with all other events — without the filter you get a large blank row aggregating everything.
Read the top keywords; terms searched often with no matching product point to assortment gaps or merchandising/labeling improvements.
caveats: The site-search event name depends on your setup; the exact name 'view search results' is specific to the demo property.
Requires the site-search event parameters to be captured and, if you want them in standard reports, registered as custom dimensions.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Funnel exploration: build an ecommerce funnel with breakdowns
cards.summary: Define ordered steps (view_item → add_to_cart → begin_checkout → purchase) in a funnel exploration and break them down by device to find where completion drops.
cards.use_when: Pinpointing the biggest conversion leak in your purchase path and checking whether it differs by device category.
steps: Open Explore, add a Funnel exploration, and click the pencil to edit Steps.
Define each step as an event condition: step 1 view_item, step 2 add_to_cart, step 3 begin_checkout, step 4 purchase (use your platform's actual event names).
Optional: narrow a step with a parameter (e.g. item ID) to funnel only a specific product, or by page host name/location.
Apply and read the counts of users reaching each step and the drop-off between them.
Add a breakdown dimension such as Device category to compare completion rates — the demo shows desktop completing better, hinting mobile UX is worth investigating.
Only treat ecommerce events as available if you or your platform send them; GA4 does not collect them out of the box.
caveats: Requires configured ecommerce events; absent them the funnel will have no steps to match.
Higher desktop completion is a signal to investigate, not proof of a mobile defect.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Path exploration: work backward from purchase or checkout events
cards.summary: Set the ending point to purchase or begin_checkout and read backward to reveal looping or confusing paths before conversion.
cards.use_when: Investigating why shoppers abandon checkout (e.g. logging in and out repeatedly) or what pages precede a purchase.
steps: Open Explore, add a Path exploration.
Click Start over and choose the ENDING point — e.g. event name purchase — to see what happened before the conversion.
Switch the dimension to Page path and expand backward; expect checkout pages adjacent to purchase, then keep expanding until non-checkout pages appear for useful context.
Alternatively set the starting point to begin_checkout and expand forward to watch where shoppers go; the demo shows users bouncing to account/login and back to checkout.
Interpret looping between checkout and account pages as a possible UX or login-friction problem worth testing.
caveats: Looping patterns indicate a hypothesis to investigate, not a proven cause.
Path explorations are private by default, like all explorations.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Create and register custom events and dimensions in GA4 via GTM
cards.summary: Send a custom event (e.g. menu-link click) with parameters from GTM, then register those parameters as custom dimensions to use them in reports.
cards.use_when: Tracking a store interaction GA4 does not collect automatically — e.g. clicks on a homepage banner, nav menu, or a category tile you want to evaluate.
steps: In GTM create a trigger (e.g. Just Links) and use Preview to identify the click; inspect the Variables panel for click text, click URL and click classes.
If click-related variables are missing, enable them under Variables > Configure > Click variables.
Narrow the trigger with click classes contains a class value that identifies the element (e.g. nav link) — inspect your own site's classes since these differ by site.
Create a tag: Google Analytics > GA4 event, paste the measurement ID, name the event in lowercase with underscores (GA4 event names must be lowercase, no spaces).
Add event parameters (e.g. menu_item_name = click text, menu_item_url = click URL) using GTM variables.
Attach the tag to the trigger, name and save it, then test through GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView before publishing.
In GA4, register each custom parameter as a custom dimension (Admin > Custom definitions > Create custom dimension) with scope Event so it appears in reports and explorations.
Publish the GTM container after successful testing.
caveats: Custom dimensions only appear in standard reports after the event is sent and data has processed (roughly 24–48 hours).
Parameter and event names are case-sensitive and must match exactly between GTM, GA4 registration and filters.
Verify current GTM/GA4 menus, which change over time.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Configure five settings in every new GA4 property
cards.summary: Day-one GA4 configuration: event data retention to 14 months, cross-domain tracking, session timeout, engaged-session threshold, and internal traffic exclusions.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new store property or fixing a recently created one where exploration history is short or sessions split unnaturally.
steps: 1. Data retention: Admin > Data retention, change event data retention from the default 2 months to 14 months (Premium can go longer). Explorations only see data within the retention window, so set this at property creation.

2. Multiple domains: if one property covers several domains, tell GA4 which domains belong to your business and configure cross-domain tracking in the data stream settings so sessions join across domains.
3. Session timeout: extend the default session duration (the demo property is 30 minutes) if leaving-mid-checkout breaks sessions into a new session with checkout as the landing page.
4. Engaged sessions: the presenter recommends raising the default 10-second engaged-session threshold to at least 30 seconds to better reflect real store engagement.
5. Internal traffic: exclude your own/team IP addresses so staff visits and test orders do not pollute revenue and conversion data.
caveats: Thresholds (10s default, 30s recommendation, 30-minute session timeout) are the presenter's guidance, not absolutes; choose values that fit how your shoppers buy.
Premium (360) allows longer retention; the standard limit is 14 months.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Use Analytics Advisor cautiously for quick questions
cards.summary: The Gemini-powered Analytics Advisor answers natural-language questions about your GA4 data, but hallucinates on technical causes.
cards.use_when: Getting a fast number from your own GA4 property (e.g. purchases from organic search last week) without building an exploration.
steps: Open the Analytics Advisor icon in the GA4 interface and type a question, e.g. 'How many purchases came from organic search in the last week?'
Verify the answer against the source report it references (e.g. the traffic acquisition report) and check the date range it applied matches your question.
Rely on it for simple numeric lookups where you can independently confirm the result.

Do NOT trust its explanations of why data looks a certain way — the demo shows it asserting a myth that firing a custom event before page_view causes 'not set' landing pages (the presenter's testing shows this is false).
caveats: Feature is in beta and powered by Gemini; it can hallucinate, cite wrong sources and opens reports with incorrect date ranges.
Useful for experienced users as a time-saver; the presenter warns it can mislead complete beginners.
Verify the current interface and beta status before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Demographics, tech and region reports for audience context
cards.summary: Use user attributes and tech detail reports to see where shoppers are and what they browse on, treating demographics as directional.
cards.use_when: Shaping merchandising, shipping or site-experience decisions — e.g. localising assortment by region or prioritising mobile experience.
steps: In User attributes > Demographic details, view country, region or city of shoppers to spot core markets.
If Google signals is enabled you may also see age, gender and interests — treat these three as imprecise and directional only.
In Tech > Tech details, view browser performance and switch the dimension to operating system or device category.
Cross-check device/tech findings against the checkout journey and funnel reports to confirm whether a given device or browser truly under-converts.
caveats: Demographic dimensions (age/gender/interests) are not highly accurate and require Google signals.
Report collection names vary by the business objectives chosen at setup.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx
